utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Registrar, good morning to you. I very kindly ask you to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Are you hearing me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I hear and I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the Prosecution, appearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, assisted by Hasan Younis, case manager. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm here with Milan Tesovic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. I understand there are no preliminaries. You have your schedule for the rest of the week, for this week. We're working today in the morning, and the next four days in the afternoon. All right? Okay, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, except we won't be working for the next four days. I mean, we're going to finish by Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I meant to say is I just wanted you to know what the schedule is in case --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. One of the Rule 92 witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- isn't coming this week, and I can't remember which one it is at the moment. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was working on that over the weekend, and in fact either later on today or first thing tomorrow I was -- I meant to come back to you on the Rule 92, all right? But we had a problem with 7.192. That's the one with the medical certificate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Et cetera. And I think that's the position is reserved also perhaps pending -- the next one was going to be --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, one of them can't come this week, Your Honour, and I have to go and check which one it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let me know and then we'll take it up from there. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you'll recall that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- that I requested leave until today to speak to you about the Rule 92 bis thing. On, I think it was Friday night, I found in the transcript where with regard to 7.191 and 7.192 I had specifically said that Brdjanin had no objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In fact one of the things I was going to point out to you was precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- either one of those, and therefore it is I think more difficult for me to assert that I now want them here, although I would like to think that had I not known the position that General Talic's counsel had taken, that I may have taken a different position, but I can't say that myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have gone through their statements. I have gone through their statements, and I don't quite think that you would have changed your position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also I did go through it accurately, even though I didn't really have to, accurately over Talic's objection at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've done both things, Your Honour, and I really -- I don't know that I would -- I will not continue insisting that they be brought here, frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it would just waste all of our time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So good morning to you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do I understand that I don't now -- because 7.191 was the gentleman who couldn't come until later because he didn't have a passport. So I'm now taking it I don't have to bring him or 7.192.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You don't need to bring him, as I understand it, 7.191.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two the same. But 2 we had a problem with the medical certificate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He was being summoned also only for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So the position is also that you don't need to bring him over, as I take it. I stand to be corrected if I'm misinterpreting you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're not, Your Honour. You're correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So good morning to you, and welcome back. I hope you had a tranquil weekend and that you're tasting a little bit of the weather in The Hague, which is just progressively getting worse, but you will be back home before it really gets worse. So we will continue with your testimony today, and before we do so, may I kindly ask you to stand up. The usher is going to hand you the same solemn declaration that you saw last Friday. And may I kindly ask you to repeat that solemn declaration, to tell us the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Ms. Korner. Examined by Ms. Korner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go back please to the, for a moment, official note which we finished looking at last Thursday, dated the 17th of June, which I believe was given an exhibit number. I can't remember what it is now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. P1113

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that, do you remember we looked at the fact that there was a reference in that to guard duty in local communes. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That's all that I wanted to remind ourselves of that. But I want you to have a look at another document now. Could you look at P1061.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's no volume 3, Your Honours, of the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Egrlic, I think you had a chance to have a look at that when you were going through various documents before you testified. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think it's equally right, this apparently was some kind of a diary kept by a gentleman named Edin Hodzic, and you don't know him?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want to ask you about is some things that he records in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that diary. If we look, please, at the entry for the 2nd of May, 1992, where there is an entry relating to a young Muslim man being killed in Kljuc the previous evening. Do you remember the killing of a young Muslim man in Kljuc around the 1st of May?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was he said to have been killed by?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: After the killing, the police came out to conduct an investigation, and they claimed that he was killed by a person from the army, a member of the Serb army reserves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it goes on to talk about an ultimatum being given to the people in Vrhpolje to hand over weapons. Do you remember that ultimatum being given?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: The ultimatum was not broadcast over Radio Kljuc, so I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then this man goes on to say that -- there's a bit of bad language, and then: "They really want war. Well, then, they will have it. It's just that they have much more weapons than we do." Would you agree that was an accurate estimation?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then if we move on to the 7th of May, that deals -- it reports the takeover, the army being stationed between Pudin Han and Kljuc, and Kljuc itself as well. And then if we move to the 15th of May, please -- I'm sorry, the 10th of May. He records: "We have until 1500 hours tomorrow to hand over weapons in the Kljuc municipality." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then he talks about on the 15th of May seeing the Serbian mentality -- the Serbian flag hoisted on the municipality building. And then on the 28th of May, he talks about the shelling of Vrhpolje. By the 28th of May, you had been arrested; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I was arrested on the 28th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before or after your arrest, did you hear about the shelling at Vrhpolje?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I heard that there were -- there was shooting in Sanski Most and that the first Bosniaks had been arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then the rest of the diary is a description of events which happened after your arrest. Yes. Thank you. If you can put that away. And now could you have a look, please, at another document that is actually entitled "Guard Duty."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was attached to the statement and was on the list. Your Honours got copies of it. It was in that bundle that we handed in, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, first of all, Mr. Egrlic, is this a document that you had seen before? It appears to be some kind of an announcement or something that went out on Kljuc radio.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: This is a part of a document. I think that I did see it before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you able to help us as to what it is at all? It talks about talking to you in the third paragraph. It appears to be some kind of a reporter.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I think this is a journalist from Radio Kljuc. I had the conversation with him so that he would be able to inform the public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I know it's difficult, but can you remember roughly when this was? Because there's no date on it.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: It could have been in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, it begins by saying that "In The past two days, stories about guard duty in the area of Krasulje and Pudin Han have been circulating around Kljuc municipality. We could not obtain any information from official organs and the public security station because they had been officially instructed that any communication with the public was to be carried out through the official spokesman, whom we could not reach. However, we talked to the presidents of the SDA and the MBO, Asim Egrlic and Omer Filipovic, who told us it was true that people had stood guard and been on duty during holidays and some cars had even been stopped and passengers asked to present their identity cards in Donji Krasulje, and but this had all been done by citizens of Muslim nationality who had organised themselves on their own initiative because of everything that had been going on in the country and because of possible acts of provocation in BH territory." It's not true that guard duty was organised on the orders of activists from these parties. This was complete disinformation. It is true, however, that activists went out in the field before and during the holidays, pointing out that it was necessary to be on heightened alert but not to organise people to stand guard and be on duty. SDA and MBO representatives told us that Muslim people --" and then, "As regards barricades, we were told that was too strong a word for what had happened. SDA and MBO representatives told us that the Muslim people had a reason to be on the alert because they could be the scapegoat in the conflict between Serbs and Croats," and so on. Now, first of all, is that, from what you recall, an accurate report of what you and Mr. Filipovic said?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I think that it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you just explain: It talks about a holiday. Which holiday was that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It talks about holidays.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or holidays. Sorry. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: According to the last sentence, it's possible that this was in 1991, and we are probably talking about the November holidays here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The November holidays being what?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: The 29th of November is statehood day, so that day is not a working day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Mr. Egrlic. You can put that document away now. I'm going to ask you to look at in a moment at the statement that you actually signed at Manjaca, but before I do that, I want to go back over one thing, when I check the transcript. You told us about the army, and we saw it in that diary being stationed in the Kljuc area, around Laniste and between Pudin Han and Kljuc town. You told us that there were the Knin Corps. Were you familiar with a part of the army called the 6th Krajina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at this period of time, so May 1992, were they stationed anywhere in Kljuc that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: They came to Kljuc on the 7th of May and they were distributed at all the important checkpoints around Kljuc, all the important places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you know they were the 6th Krajina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Because they came from the direction of Sanski Most. That's where they were stationed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was there anything about their insignia that established who they were?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Just like with the police, the insignia was changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, I want you to have a look, please, at the actual statement that you signed in Manjaca. I think it's headed -- yes. It's headed "Manjaca prisoner of war camp" and dated the 29th of June. It was attached to the statement when it was handed to Your Honours. It's attached, for the purpose of Madam -- it was attached to the bundle of statements that were handed in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's 03039891; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right. I'm just waiting while the registry find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was attached to the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's attached to the statement. It's a totally separate bundle. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Your Honour, we've got our copy. If the witness has the version in B/C/S and if you can put the English on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us on Thursday, Mr. Egrlic, about the beatings which had taken place before and after the interrogations. First of all, is that your signature at the bottom of the statement?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I think that it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of state were you in when you signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I had been taken from the stables, where we were placed. I had been taken out from there several times to provide a statement. Before that, all of those who were to provide statements would be beaten, and that was the state we were in while providing statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity before you signed to read through what was contained in the statement?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I didn't read it because they kept telling us to hurry up, so that I signed it without reading it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there a number of you at the same time being brought in to sign statements?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I was alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we just look at the contents, then? It's dated the 29th of June, 1992, Manjaca prisoner of war camp, military secret, strictly confidential. And the first paragraph says that: "During May of 1992, I attended a meeting in Sanski Most. Omer Filipovic and I went to the meeting," and I'm summarising it: The meeting was convened and held at the initiative of representatives from Sanski Most, and the following people also attended the meeting: Redzo Kurbegovic and Mirzet Karabeg. And the secretary and one or two people I did not know. At the meeting there was discussion of the general situation in the Republic and problems of a similar nature in the municipality, related to changes in the police insignia and suspension of the municipal organs, et cetera. It was believed the events might lead to a deterioration in relations since a request for weapons to be surrendered is expected from the Crisis Staff in Sanski Most. The meeting did not adopt any official conclusions, but it was said that the appointed staff of the BH Territorial Defence should request a display of loyalty to BH and they should be ready for defence in the event of a possible attack. In this respect, the two municipalities might possibly act together since they border one another. Mr. Egrlic, first, was there such a meeting in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were the discussions as set out here?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: There were discussions and general concern was expressed about situation, but there was no possibility of cooperation, because checkpoints had already been set up at all the junctions there. And throughout the municipality of Kljuc, as well as in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you tell your interrogators in Manjaca that there was a possibility that the municipalities might act together at that stage?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I said that we had held a meeting and we expressed concern for the citizens' safety, but there was no talk of any form of cooperation whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the next part of that statement deals with events in Kljuc on the 27th of May, and in effect, it's very much as the record of interrogation that you and Mr. Filipovic had come to the centre in Pudin Han to connect the telephone and the fax machine. And then you heard about the incident in Krasulje and Omer Filipovic went off there and discovered that a policeman had been killed and another wounded. First, is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you apparently were surprised and confused, went home to your family, and then you all fled because of the shooting, and you then left your family and went to Pudin Han to find out what was happening, where you found Omer, and that's what happened, was it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you heard about the shelling of Velagici, you went to spend the night with someone else, and then you accidentally wounded yourself. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think that's been exhibited yet. May that be made P1114.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us about the beatings. When did the beatings actually start? At Manjaca, I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: There were beatings on a daily basis, so you can't really say where the beginning was, or the end, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You arrived at Manjaca sometime in mid-June. When was actually the first time that you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: The first time, just like everyone else, I was beaten as soon as I arrived, when they called out our names and when we were brought into the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know the name of the man who beat you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I did find out later, the first day after our arrival. Of course, I didn't know at first, but while I was there I got to learn the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the name of the man?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: His nickname was Fadil.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever discover what his real name was?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but right now I can't seem to remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he beat you with?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: He beat me with a club which was made out of wire -- it was made out of a cable, and he used this club to beat prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what injuries did you suffer as a result of that beating?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Both at that time and later, I was beaten on my back. My ribs were broken and my collarbone was broken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to get any medical treatment at the camp?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Not for those who were beaten. Those were not administered any medical assistance, nor was I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If people were seeking medical treatment and waiting outside the, as it were, makeshift surgery, what would happen to them?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Normally, those guards who would take people to the medical station to receive medical assistance, those were the people who would be beaten, both on the way to the medical station and on the way back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the camp commander?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you are aware, was he ever present when beatings were happening?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Not that I know of. Mostly it was the guards who beat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it's right: You were in Manjaca until December. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, or thereabouts. To the best of my recollection, I think it was the 13th of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you a few questions, please, about the conditions at Manjaca. First of all, before the arrival the Red Cross, what sort of food were you getting?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Before the arrival of the Red Cross, we had, well, I'm not sure you could really call that a meal. It was some sort of a soup, and a slice of bread each, which would then be cut up into 30 or more pieces. We kept losing weight, so both myself and the other prisoners, some of us lost over 20 kilos in just two months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about sanitation facilities?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Well, the sanitation facilities, I'm not sure you could really talk about that. That was gruelling. Those were stables over there where people would be put up. Of course, there was cattle being kept in those stables before we came. So on some parts of the ground, you had hay covering the ground, and there were blankets in some spots. As far as the toilet facilities are concerned, we had field privies, and the situation in those privies was horrible. Order was brought by taking ten prisoners Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. at a time to the field privy to relieve themselves. As far as water is concerned, water would be brought from a nearby lake. So during summer, people would have three sips of water each, because there was not enough water for all the inmates. There wasn't enough water to be supplied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the arrival of the Red Cross, did conditions improve?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: After the arrival of the Red Cross, conditions improved as far as food was concerned. Food supply continued, and then the size of the meals improved. So food, generally speaking, improved after the arrival of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the beatings continue after the arrival of the Red Cross or did they stop?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, the beatings continued. Beatings became particularly severe after people's names were called out, so that people would be taken to perform labour in the woods or in the fields.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say it became particularly severe after their names had been called out. Do you mean the beatings took place on the way to labour?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: This did take place very often indeed, but I do remember one particularly impressive or, should I say, dreadful event, when there weren't enough people to volunteer. Then they would just herd all the inmates outside the stables, where they were being held, and they would start beating them. During those beatings, I received a blow with a wooden plank over my right shoulder, and that's when my collarbone broke. This was the sort of repression they used to force people to go outside the camp to perform labour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the death of Omer Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him before his death?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I did see him, because just before his death they had released him and brought him to a stable. He was lying there, and it was clear that he had been beaten very badly. He was pale and he looked powerless. After a while, however, they took him back to the solitary, and on the next day it was said publicly that he had died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why Omer Filipovic was particularly picked upon like this, beaten so badly?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I believe that this was so because everyone knew that he was a prominent person, a well-respected person, professor of history. Everyone knew that he had been appointed head of the TO staff for Kljuc municipality and that that was the reason why they would take him away and beat him and why they wanted statements from him. He didn't survive. He succumbed to the result of those beatings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay at the camp, if that's the right word, did you see any of the politicians from Banja Luka at the camp?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, on one occasion, one of the politicians arrived and he gave a speech to the inmates, saying that the whole thing would be over very soon and that people would be released and free to return to their homes. He imbued people with a false sense of confidence, because long after he had been there, people stayed on in the camp. Some died. Some never returned to their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who it was?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I think it was the president of the municipality -- of the Municipal Assembly of the Autonomous Region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise him, or were you just told who he was?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No. I think that's who he said he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he told you he was what? The president of --?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: The Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, have you had any lasting results or any lasting effects, I should say, of what was done to you in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I have headaches all the time and a buzzing sound in my ears, pain in my chest, and my spine was damaged, due to which I had to undergo an operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to look at a few documents that relate to the period when you were in Manjaca but relate also to you. Could you have a look, please, first of all at the document which is a manuscript document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, it may be -- no. It's in that bundle I gave you. It's got the numbers. It's translation -- it's hand -- the original is handwritten. It's headed "Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Egrlic, there's a note on it which says this manuscript was found within the documentation of the Kljuc SJB and concerns the period immediately before the ethnic cleansing of villages with a Muslim population. Had you seen this document before you came here?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look, please, at the first page. It's dated the 10th of June, 1992 and headed "Crisis Staff," which operated before but was dissolved immediately before the armed conflicts, Muhamed Filipovic, who was in fact, I think, erroneously says the SDA. Omer Filipovic, commissioner, and then yourself, political person, and some other people are named. Now, I think you told us before that there was an idea of having a Crisis Staff but it never operated. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then look, please, at the rest of this document, leaving out the next one, the TO, 3, protection staff company, not formed but planned, and then 4, independent companies, three companies: Kljuc, Velagici, Sanica, which numbered 75 to 100 staff members. Was that an accurate assessment?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: These companies were never formed, but I think the estimate may be correct, because it was known how many able-bodied men of military age were in the area at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it goes on. There were four platoons, and names the four places where they were. Were there platoons, four platoons?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No. There was nothing, no guards, as I said before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then I'm not going to take you through all of this document, but it says for Velagici company, company commander Hamija Avdic [phoen] in flight. Was that correct? Did he get away?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then platoon commander -- sorry. Ekrem Cehic, prison. Did you know this man?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know Ekrem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any of the people named on this page?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Is this page 7 we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's under -- if you look under -- it's the first -- it has Velagici at the top and then Krasulje in the middle of the page. It's the third page of the document.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Velagici and then Krasulje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to know whether there were any people on that page who you knew.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I knew Salih Salihovic and Nevzad Djeric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This says that they're in prison.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When it referred to "prison," do you know what it referred to, which prison? For example, were any of the people on this page in Manjaca with you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: All these people were. Salih Salihovic, Nevzad Djeric, in flight, Enes Salihovic, and Fahrudin Cemal they were all in the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. This appears to be some sort of record, as we can see, of happened to the various people. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think that's been exhibited yet. Could that be made P1115, 1115.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look next, please, at a document dated the 26th of June and headed "Review." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does it have a number, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. The translation L0071078.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. This is going to be P1116?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is review of executive positions held by employees of Muslim nationality. Your name comes first. I think you had a chance to look at this document the other day. But were all these people on this list in fact Muslims? For example, if you go, please, to where we come to Sana-Kljuc, the director?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Director Drasko Banjac. He was a Serb, but he was married to a Muslim woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these people, the Muslims who were named here, did all of them lose their jobs?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Roughly how many of them were, if you can tell us -- if we just, for example, look at the Municipal Assembly Kljuc, how many of these people were arrested? The very first page.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I was arrested, secretary of the executive committee, Fikret Balagic, was killed, Mrs. Filipovic was not arrested, Hamdija Ducanovic was not arrested either. From this list I was the only one to be arrested, and Mr. Fikret Balagic was killed. All the others on this list were fired and they were left without a job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was Mr. Balagic killed?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Balagic was killed in Biljani, alongside with the other locals from Biljani, and he was found together with his neighbours in a pit on Laniste after their arrival in Kljuc in 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Could you look now, please, at a document dated the 21st of July and headed "Ruling."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The number, Your Honour, is 01107624. Your Honour, perhaps -- I'm sorry. Perhaps it may have been -- it was attached to the statement. Perhaps I can just show it and we'll make copies. If that can go on the ELMO. Actually, if we put it on the ELMO, that will do, and give the B/C/S to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's dated the 21st of July and it states that the Kljuc Municipal Assembly or War Presidency passed a ruling to relieve the chairman of the Kljuc municipality of his duty, the executive committee of his duty, Asim Egrlic the current chairman of the Kljuc municipality executive committee will be relieved of his duty as chairman on the 1st of June, 1992, and it's signed by the president of the War Presidency, Jovo Banjac. By the 1st of June, 1992, where were you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: From the 28th onwards I was detained at the camp, from the 28th of May onwards. That's when I was at the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I'm afraid it was missed off my list, but perhaps that could be made Exhibit P1117 and we'll provide copies after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now could you have a look, please, at a document dated the 3rd of August, 1992. I'm sorry. Before that, could you have a look at a document dated -- it's headed "List of persons from Pudin Han and Velagici." The number is O0064776, I think. It's a list of -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is going to be 1117?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 1118, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's headed "List of persons from Pudin Han and Velagici," and we see there your name as number 4, your function, SDA president weapons. It alleges that you had this submachine-gun, or I think it's called a Zagi, and a pistol. Was that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: It's true that I had a pistol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But not the other weapon?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No. Just the pistol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Then status: Processed, result prison; remark, dealt with political issues." Do you know -- apart from the obvious ones, like Omer Filipovic, do you know the other people on the list? For example, number 13?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you had better tell us: Which ones on the list did you know?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I knew the late Omer, Amir, Nevzad, Salih, Enes, Fahrudin, Hilmo Draganovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under number 7, Enes Salihovic it says: "Function, highest leadership." What sort of function did Mr. Salihovic have?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he had a private printing press, but he wasn't part of the leadership, part of any leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It alleges that he organised the ammunition supply and prepared an ambush for the police. Are you aware of him doing anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now could we have a look, please, and just two more documents, first of all at a document dated the 3rd of August, 1992. The numbers are L0063751. It's headed -- yes- "Commission for gathering information on resettlement of the population." This apparently is a record compiled on the 3rd of August, in the offices of Kljuc municipality, regarding a declaration of means given by Sabiha Egrlic before permanently leaving the territory of Kljuc municipality of her own free will. Who was Sabiha Egrlic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: That was my wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It goes on to say who was present and then says: "The party Egrlici approached this organ without having been summoned and after being informed of the order of War Presidency of Kljuc municipality setting up criteria for permanent departure." And then she made a declaration that she possesses the following immovable property and gives a description and that "I am leaving Kljuc municipality with my family for good, of my own free will, and I have made this statement without coercion and in full consciousness of my words, for the purpose of obtaining documents for permanent resettlement and departure from Kljuc municipality." Were you aware of what your -- did you become aware of what your wife had done?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: My wife, just like all the others who had to leave the municipality of Kljuc, had to sign such statements that they were leaving all of their property to Republika Srpska, and they had to also make all of the payments that were outstanding, for example, outstanding telephone bills, electricity bills, taxes, and they also had to sign a statement that they were giving up their property. Only then could they leave the area of the Kljuc municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she leave of her own free will?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: She had to. She didn't go of her own free will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could that, please, be made P1119.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you returned to Kljuc in 1995, I think it was, what had happened to your property?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: When I came back to Kljuc, all my property was completely destroyed, just like the property of the majority of Bosniaks from the municipality of Kljuc. My house was burned, my car also. I practically had nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The final document I want you to look at.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is already an exhibit. It is P1101, I think. Your Honour, we looked at it with Mr. Filipovic. Could he be handed the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is dated the 9th of June, 1995, headed "The Republika Srpska public security station in Kljuc." And it's a criminal report being filed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. against you, amongst other people, in respect of what is described later as, I think, armed rebellion. Yes. If we look -- it's you and 238 other people, and if we look under -- if you look under 239th you'll see on grounds of reasonable suspicion, having committed the gravest form of the crime of armed rebellion. There's then a description of what's said to be the allegations. Were you aware that in June of 1995 a criminal report had been filed against you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I didn't know about this. I found out about it when I came to Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how much longer after this - this is dated June of 1995 - did you return to Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I came back to Kljuc in late September 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now finally this, Mr. Egrlic: You've told us that you came back to find your property, your house, destroyed, and that of other Muslims. What about mosques in Kljuc? Were any standing?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: All the mosques in the municipality of Kljuc were knocked down, as well as the facilities which were used for the housing of religious officials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a Catholic church or Catholic churches -- well, first of all, in Kljuc town was there a Catholic church?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: There was one, but that also was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Muslims were left in the municipality when you returned in September of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: About 600 Muslims, Muslim Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many roughly? We've got some figures, but how many were there before the events of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: According to the census, there were about 17.700 in the region of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And over the next really years, were you present at a number of exhumations that took place throughout the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I went to all the places where mass graves were found. The first one that was discovered was the so-called Crvena Zemlja location, red earth, then Babina Dolina at Laniste, then Bezdana at Laniste. Then there was the mass grave at Prhovo. And the last mass grave that was discovered was at Ratkovo where people from the Humici local community were found. Citizens from Biljani, Velagici, Kljuc were found in these mass graves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Egrlic. Can you wait there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. We've got about eight minutes before the break. Would you prefer to start now and then break after eight minutes or break now and resume after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's probably easier to break now and start after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I ask Mr. Ackerman, it's simply the next witness, whether we'll get to the next witness today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's just almost impossible for me to say. I guess I'd have to say there is a possibility we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's simply whether we bring him to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My rough guess is that we might start with him. So I would suggest, Ms. Korner, that you bring him over for after the next break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I'm pretty sure that he will take up the next hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, by the next break I'll have a real good idea how much longer I'll be, I'm sure and then we can make that decision, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just didn't want to put him in the witness waiting room unnecessarily. So we'll wait until the next break and let him know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a break now, and then Mr. Ackerman for Mr. Brdjanin will start examining you immediately after. The break is for 25 minutes please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. We're having a problem here with computers, but we seem to have one that's working, so it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think so. This one has stopped completely, but it's -- the other one seems to be working still. All right. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whenever it's convenient.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I just remind you, sir, of something I told you last Friday when you started giving evidence, and you are going to be cross-examined by the lead counsel for the accused in this case. This is a right that is given by the law, by our Rules in particular, to any accused, to have witnesses brought forward by the Prosecution cross-examined by the Defence for the accused, and your duty is to treat counsel for the accused the same as you've treated the counsel for the Prosecution, and your duty is to answer all questions truthfully, unless we tell you not to answer a particular question. Mr. Ackerman, the witness is in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to have a number of questions to ask you, and to the extent that it's possible, please try to confine your answers to yes or no, because I intend to ask you some questions that can easily be answered that way. There will also be questions where you will have to make some explanations, but I think the differential should be clear to you. Okay? I'm going to ask you a series of questions that arise from the testimony you gave here last week, and I want to begin with -- you will recall that you had before you last week a document which was a telex or fax that you said had come from somewhere, but it had Mr. Brdjanin's name on it, and it appeared to be some instructions, and you had kept a copy of it, but it had gotten burned up in your house, and the document we're talking about is Prosecution's Exhibit P22. Do you recall that document?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were asked by Ms. Korner - and this is at page 32 of the transcript - "There are in there a set of instructions. Were those instructions actually put into effect?" Your answer was: "They were." The question then: "All of them or just some of them, if you can remember?" Your answer: "Most of them were implemented from 1991 right up until May 1992." And I'd ask that you be shown that exhibit, P22, please. I want to go through each paragraph and ask you a question about each one. We'll start with paragraph 1. First of all, this is a document dated 29 October 1991, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 1 says: "Immediately form a command of the town and set up round-the-clock duty." Was that paragraph implemented immediately after 29 October 1991?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if immediately, but later on, yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, later on would have been 1992, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I found out about it in early 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm just putting the English version on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm just asking the usher to put the English version on the ELMO so that the public can follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 2: "Establish full mobility of the Territorial Defence." Do you know if that was done?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: From mid-1991 onwards, there were permanent mobilisations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Form units for the front and designate their replacements." Do you know if that was done?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: This was done when the units of the Knin Corps arrived at Laniste.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: That was in March 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Five months after this document?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: At the time of this document, there were units of volunteers who went to Croatia to take part in the war there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 4: "All men under the age of 40 to be reassigned from civilian protection to the Territorial Defence, and the Territorial Defence to be resubordinated to the corps as wartime units." Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that, because I didn't see any evidence or documents about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 5: "Take over management in public enterprises, the post office, SDK, bank, judiciary, and, by all means, the media." Was that done?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, during April and May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, six -- around six months after this document; correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 6: "Proclaim a wartime programme schedule on radio stations." Was that done?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: That was also done in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 7: "In each municipality, call a meeting of all directors and agree on the means of supplying the population with everything from electricity to consumer goods." Do you know if that happened?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: There were several meetings, as far as businessmen from the Kljuc area are concerned, during 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those meetings have to do with agreement on the means of supplying the population with everything from electricity to consumer goods?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: In the second half of 1991, restriction measures had already been introduced with regard to the supply of fuel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at number 8, please: "Place a moratorium on the issuing of construction permits, sale of plots/of land, election of directors, where the absence of reservists is being abused, and halt all changes of ownership of enterprises, et cetera." Was that done?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether this has been implemented completely, fully, but I do know that SDS leaders worked -- built business premises, buildings used for business premises, to house business premises, with no permission whatsoever, in the very centre of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was ignored; correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I don't think it was ignored. It was done with tacit consent. There was no intervention to keep this from happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, there was a big dispute about that in the Assembly, wasn't there, that you were involved in, regarding construction permits or something, where you withdrew from the Assembly because of refusal to discuss it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: That may have been in March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Number 10: "All weapons and equipment to be collected from deserters." Do you know if that happened?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they collected the weapons from those deserters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 11: "Make lists of surplus goods, as well as shortages, and inform SDS Sarajevo, Mr. Ilic, about this." Do you know if that was done?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 12: "Paramilitary formations, if they exist, to be disbanded immediately and reassigned to the Territorial Defence. This must be carried out without fail." Was that done?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. They continued to be independent and not under anyone's command, a number of groups which intimidated the population by shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 13: "Impose also war taxes for greater success of the entire operation." Was that done?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know, except that meetings were held with directors of companies, and that they were requested to provide assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about war taxes; correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 14: "Request Radio Banja Luka to broadcast one hour of programme time daily on the war events in Croatia." Would the authorities in Kljuc have had any authority to request Radio Banja Luka to do anything?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: They practically put together the programme schedule for Radio Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But not Radio Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you told the Judges that most of these were carried out, what you really meant was maybe one or two of them, and probably in 1992; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I thought that when I said "most of them," I was referring to the most important of these items, and those indeed were implemented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document is not signed by Mr. Brdjanin, is it? There's no signature on it.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any other document in which Mr. Brdjanin was designated a coordinator?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I did. A document with this content, but not any other document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is the only document you've seen in which he was designated a coordinator?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that a coordinator is simply a person who coordinates between bodies and has no authority in their own right? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm finished with that document for now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your testimony - it's page 32, line 17 - you were asked if you had any other conversations with any of the leadership of the SDS about Mr. Brdjanin. After a couple of other asides, your answer was this: "Not directly, but I heard from SDS representatives that Brdjanin was highly respected in the SDS and that he was deeply appreciated." That was your answer; correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were these SDS representatives that you heard that from? What were their names?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I heard this from Jovo Banjac and Veljko Kondic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I heard this on several occasions, especially in early 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're telling us that you heard from Jovo Banjac that Brdjanin was highly respected and deeply appreciated; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also told us, on the same page, in line 7, that when you asked Jovo Banjac about this document, P22, he said: "Never mind that. Brdjo is crazy." Right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to now be handed Exhibit 853.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Put the English on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a document with two versions on the same sheet of paper. So do we have it on the ELMO? Yes, we have. All right. The English version. Please go ahead, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, we discussed this document when you testified the other day. You discussed it. I want to specifically refer you to the last paragraph. First of all, just to kind of set the scene here, this was June 9th of 1991, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is a document jointly authored by you and Omer Filipovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last paragraph of that document, you say this: "We call on all patriots to unite in the struggle to preserve the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina, regardless of their ethnic, religious, or political affiliation." Now, at that time, Bosnia-Herzegovina was part of Yugoslavia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, but at that time, volunteers started to leave for Croatia, to fight there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what was going on in Croatia was an effort to preserve the sovereignty Yugoslavia by keeping Croatia from seceding, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No. That was an attempt to create Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's your take on it, but Croatia was trying to secede from Yugoslavia and an effort was being made to keep that from happening; isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's not true that Croatia wanted to be independent?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: It wanted to be independent after negotiations on the status of former Yugoslavia had failed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you're calling for by this document is you're calling for people to revolt against what's going on. Patriots should unite, the Muslims should unite, take up arms; correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. It reads, clearly: "Regardless of their ethnic, religious, or political affiliation."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll come to that a little bit later. Was there a war going on -- I'm sorry. Was there a war going on in Croatia on 9 June of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether there was a war at that time, but the so-called log revolution was already under way at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with regard to this particular document that you have before you, and that last sentence regarding the threat to sovereignty, on page 35, at line 9, you were asked this: "And what made you feel that this threatened the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina?" And your answer was this, sir: "We felt so because similar attempts were made in relation to joining Kljuc to the Bosanska Krajina region, and we felt that this could happen in the region, in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Now, you just made that answer up, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. It's true that Kljuc was joined to the Banja Luka region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in that answer, you're talking about the Autonomous Region of Krajina, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: The Autonomous Region of Krajina. This communique, we tried to draw people's attention to the fact that the same thing must be prevented from happening in Kljuc, but eventually did happen. Everyone knows that Kljuc was joined to the Banja Luka autonomous region without consulting the other ethnic groups living in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Autonomous Region of Krajina didn't exist in June of 1991, did it? No effort was being made to join Kljuc to the Autonomous Region of Krajina. It didn't exist. Right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: There was an idea, even as early as 1991, a first attempt was carried out, and the Municipal Assembly knew nothing about it. There was an attempt to join the Kljuc municipality to the Banja Luka Autonomous Region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There wasn't any Banja Luka Autonomous Region in early -- in June of 1991, was there?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date when the Autonomous Region was established, but I do know that the first annexation of the Kljuc municipality was carried out without the official organs of the Kljuc municipality being informed, and we drafted a communique, a statement to the public, about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to be shown Exhibit P858, please. Now, this document, you have it before you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document is a bit later. It's 21 September of 1991, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're making a public announcement, you and Omer Filipovic, that the Muslim residents of Kljuc shall stand under no obligation to serve in units of the reserve strength of the Yugoslav army; correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "We Bosnian Muslims do not wish and shall take no part in this war, because we do not consider the war or the Serbian/Croatian conflict our own." Correct? Now, by this document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, the interpreter did not hear your answer. Could you repeat your answer again, please. The question that was put to you was: "You're making a public announcement, you and Omer Filipovic, that the Muslim residents of Kljuc shall stand under no obligation to serve in the units of the reserve strength of the Yugoslav army; correct?" "Correct." And then you were asked: We Bosnian Muslims do not wish and shall take no part in this war, because we do not consider the war or the Serbian/Croatian conflict our own. Correct? And you answered something which the interpreter didn't catch. What is your answer, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document, sir, basically declares a revolution of the Muslim people, does it not, revolting against the legally established authorities?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doesn't it say that you're not going to follow the law and respond to a legally declared mobilisation from the government of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: At that time there was no Yugoslav People's Army already, as it had existed up until that period, since it did not have a supreme commander, and in view of the fact that the agreement on the status of the former Yugoslavia could not be formed. War was already raging in the area of the Republic of Croatia. Volunteers went from the region of Kljuc, and they would come back and disturb the population in the municipality of Kljuc, and these were the reasons why we addressed the public and said that we did not wish to push Bosniaks into such a war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were advising Bosniaks to violate the law, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: At that time already, as far as a joint Yugoslav army was concerned, an army of Yugoslavia, it wasn't functioning at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say there was no supreme commander, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I mean that there was chaos in the ranks of the Yugoslav People's Army because of the very fact that there was a war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say there was no supreme commander? There was, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: There was one, but he didn't have any jurisdiction over the army, any powers over the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who would that have been?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: According to the constitution, it should have been the Presidency of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why do you say the Presidency of Yugoslavia had no control over the army?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: It did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I say that because volunteers from the municipality of Kljuc went to the front in Croatia. This was not the policy of the former Yugoslavia or of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm finished with that document. I'd like you to look at P860, please. Now, this again, sir, is a document that is authored by you, dated 21 September 1991, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's a document basically issued by the town board of the SDA, over your signature; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there was -- there were multiparty elections held in Kljuc, and the SDS won the majority of seats in the Municipal Assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what you're saying here, sir, is it not, that the Municipal Assembly of Kljuc is voting to take certain steps that you don't agree with, and that if they continue to take these steps that you don't agree with, then you'll split off and form your own Muslim commune; correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you lost the election, but if things don't go your way, then you'll go on your own; in other words, you're not paying any attention to democratic principles and following the will of the majority, are you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: We're talking about one issue here, and this public statement arises from that issue, was issued because of that, and that's obvious from item 4. So the SDS alone, without an Assembly session, agreed to join the municipality of Kljuc to the Banja Luka-Krajina Autonomous Region, and this meant that it was a question of secession from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the creation of Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, there were actually at least a couple of incidents, sir, where you took this position. One was you had asked for an investigation into, I think, the issuance of construction permits and had made the pronouncement that if the majority did not go along with your demand in that regard that you would leave the assembly and form your own commune. And then when the majority wanted to join the autonomous district of Krajina, you made the announcement that if they didn't go along with what you wanted in the minority, that you would leave the assembly and form your own commune. In other words, what you were saying, sir, wasn't it, that we lost the election, we won't accept what the majority wants, we'll form our own commune, we won't accept a democratic government in Kljuc; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about the vital interests of the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina regarding whether they should remain in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Serbs, on the other hand, who wished to join the former Yugoslavia, that's how it is. So we issued this statement in that context, making it known that we still wish to be committed citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what you did was announce that you were engaging in a revolt against the duly elected government, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: That is your interpretation. My interpretation is that we wanted the following: If there was no agreement on vital interests, then we wanted to have a new municipality established, and that in that context we wished to have a peaceful region and peaceful cooperation. This was our objective. As far as the municipality of Bosanski Kljuc is concerned, this never actually materialised. It was just a political step to make an attempt to get some sense into the other side and that they shouldn't do what they wanted to do, and that is to join the municipality of Kljuc to the region of Banja Luka and then join it to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We're going to talk about that now. I'm through with that document. On page 41 of the transcript from last week, speaking about the Autonomous Region of Krajina, you were asked this question: "You, as a Muslim in a municipality that was taken into this new separatist commune, how was that, did you think, going to affect you personally as a Muslim, if at all?" Your answer, sir, was, and I'll give you part of your answer: "This new para-state did not guarantee that the Muslims would enjoy all of their rights as citizens, and for that reason we did not want to accept to remain part of the Autonomous Region." That was your answer, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it if the rights of Muslims as citizens were guaranteed, then you would not have any objection to joining the Autonomous Region of Krajina. That follows, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: We felt that the best solution for all the peoples was to stay in the former Yugoslavia. This is something that we were in favour of, particularly the Yugoslavia which would include Serbia and Croatia. We then felt, in that case, that the interests of Bosniaks would not be jeopardised, since the war broke out in Croatia, and we didn't have any interests in remaining in the rump Yugoslavia, where as a people we would be a minority and our rights would be jeopardised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to talk to you about that and then I'll come back to my question, which you have not answered. You say that you were in favour of remaining within Yugoslavia as long as Croatia also remained within Yugoslavia. Is that what you just told us?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And yet when Yugoslavia, through the JNA, was trying to prevent the secession of Croatia, you issued a proclamation to the residents of Yugoslavia in your community who were Muslim, that they shouldn't go assist in that. Now, what is it? Did you want Croatia to be separate or not?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army never helped for Croatia to remain within Yugoslavia. Quite the contrary; it helped in the forming of Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go back to my prior question. What you said last week in your answer regarding the Autonomous Region of Krajina was this: "This new para-state did not guarantee that the Muslims would enjoy all of their rights as citizens."
